_note: PRIOR ART: none — no eval in scripts/eval/ tests advice. Disguised historical decisions, in preference order. Round 1 (names, dates and places removed, setting kept) was identified by Flash on 15 of 15 at confidence 0.95-0.99 (out/recognition-round1.jsonl, committed as recognition-round1.jsonl), so rounds 2 and 3 also move each case to another setting while keeping the decision's structure. The first ten not identified become the known-outcome stratum (known-selected.json). `case` and `risks` are never shown to the writer. The key lists what materialised in the recorded case, worded for the transposed setting. Limit, reported with the result: the outcome belongs to the original case, and the transposed story is an analogy to it. Round 2 (T*): 3 of 18 not identified. Round 3 (U*): less iconic cases, signature details removed.

candidates.text: I am chief engineer on a showpiece exhibition hall our region is building to impress foreign visitors. Part-way through the steelwork, the governor, who follows the project personally, ordered a second heavy roof terrace added high up. I have adjusted what I can. Last week a supervised trial, with workers moving as a crowd from side to side up there, made the frame sway so badly that it was stopped. Nobody in the room wants to tell the governor, who is abroad and expects the opening this summer. My career rests on it. What should I do?
risks: The structure fails soon after opening, in ordinary conditions, because it is top-heavy
People in or on it are killed
The whole investment is lost at once, with public humiliation in front of those it was meant to impress
Nobody with knowledge of the problem tells the person who ordered the change, because they fear doing so
An inquiry afterwards cannot or will not assign responsibility

candidates.text: I am a junior analyst at a care-home chain. Residents on wings served by the visiting clinical team get serious infections far more often than on the wings served only by aides. In a small trial at one home, the visiting team used a strong disinfectant between rooms and the infections fell sharply. My numbers are strong but I cannot show the mechanism, and they imply that the most senior clinicians have been harming residents. The clinical director is hostile and my contract is up for renewal. Younger colleagues urge me to go public and name names. What should I do?
risks: Senior staff reject the finding because it implies their own guilt, and the practice is dropped or not adopted
The writer's contract is not renewed, or the writer is otherwise pushed out
Failing to publish the evidence clearly and in full lets others dismiss it
Attacking colleagues angrily alienates possible allies and harms the cause
People go on dying for years because adoption is delayed
The lack of an explanation of the mechanism is used as grounds for dismissing the numbers

candidates.text: I sit on the emergency committee of a rich commercial city threatened by a huge wildfire. The business leaders here want a deliberate backburn through two rural valleys of poor smallholders, sacrificing them to protect the city and reassure investors and insurers. We can promise compensation in writing. Some fire scientists say the city might be safe anyway; others are unsure. The valley people have no real say, and could be evacuated in a few days. We could move before they organise. What should I do?
risks: The sacrifice turns out to be unnecessary, because the threat eases or breaks elsewhere
Promised compensation is paid slowly, stingily or not at all, and a long legal fight follows
The displaced communities lose homes and livelihoods for good
A lasting distrust of the city's elite and of government follows among those sacrificed
The poor bear a loss chosen by wealthy people who gain from it

candidates.text: I am a new reviewer at a national consumer-safety agency. A calming supplement for children, already popular abroad and advertised as safe for even the most sensitive users, has landed on my desk. The application looks thin: its safety data are largely testimonials, and I have seen one report of nerve damage in an adult. The company phones my superiors and visits me repeatedly, and it goes on sale automatically after a short window unless I find the file incomplete. Parents abroad swear by it. I have no proof of harm. What should I do?
risks: The product causes serious harm abroad that was not visible in the data, especially to the most vulnerable users
The company keeps up its pressure, through repeated contacts and appeals to superiors
The product reaches people here anyway, through samples or trials outside full oversight
The maker's assurance of safety for vulnerable users proves to have no real evidence behind it
The reviewer is attacked as obstructive and bureaucratic for the delay

candidates.text: I advise the president of a small coastal nation that is running out of foreign currency. Fish and shrimp farming feeds the country and earns much of its exports. He has promised a clean, natural industry, popular with voters for health reasons, and wants to ban imported manufactured feed across the sector this season. That would save hundreds of millions in hard currency at a stroke. Fisheries scientists warn of lower output, and we produce nothing like enough natural feed. Others say farmers always resist change and a gradual plan would never happen. What should I say?
risks: Output of the staple food falls steeply, so that the country must import food
A main export is badly hit, cutting the foreign earnings the ban was meant to protect
The natural substitute is not available in anything like the amount needed
Producers protest in large numbers and the government is forced into a hurried reversal
The ban deepens the wider economic crisis and political instability it was meant to ease

candidates.text: I am the state-appointed finance manager of a bankrupt school district in a poor industrial town. Switching our old school boilers to a cheap local fuel for two years, until a new heating plant is ready, would save millions and keep teachers employed. The maintenance staff say they are not ready, and the additive that protects old boilers from that fuel is a cost we did not budget for. Air tests are coming up, and airing out the classrooms just before sampling would help us pass. Parents distrust everything I do. What should I do?
risks: The cheap source corrodes old equipment and releases a poison that harms children
Illness spreads and some people die
Officials dismiss complaints for months, and manipulated or misleading sampling hides the problem
The savings are dwarfed by the eventual cost of repairs and settlements
Criminal charges and lasting loss of trust follow for officials

candidates.text: I am a senior manager at an old, respected farmers' co-operative. A young grain buyer in a distant depot is producing astonishing profits on forward contracts, and he is about to account for a fifth of our earnings. Because the depot is small, he both makes the contracts and keeps the books that record them. Our auditors have suggested separating those roles, but that costs money and could upset our star just as bonuses are being set. The board is delighted and wants to send him more capital. I have no evidence of wrongdoing. What should I do?
risks: The trader hides losses in the records he himself controls
The hidden losses grow rapidly until they exceed the organisation's capital and it collapses
Management sends more money to him without understanding how the profits are made
Warnings from audit go unacted upon
Staff and owners lose jobs, savings and an old name, with executives publicly blamed

candidates.text: For twenty years I have quietly gathered evidence for a theory that would overturn the central assumption of my field of economics, and would upset my family and the community I grew up in, who hold to the old view as a matter of faith. My health collapses whenever I work on it. Friends tell me to publish a short sketch now, because others may be getting close. I would rather finish the great book, with all the proofs, so that it cannot be dismissed. That might take many more years. What should I do?
risks: Someone else reaches the same idea independently and threatens the writer's priority
The writer is then forced to publish in a rush, in a shorter and less finished form than planned
The full, perfected work is never completed
Publication brings attack from religious or public opinion
The strain on health and family continues whichever course is taken

candidates.text: I administer a growing lakeside city where an invasive crayfish has infested the new drainage canals and threatens the rice fields around us. Paid crews cannot keep pace. A clerk suggests a bounty for each crayfish killed by residents, who are poor and would welcome the money. To keep costs down and spare our offices the carcasses, they would only have to hand in a claw. Some of my colleagues find this demeaning; others worry about the expense. It would be simple to launch next week. What should I do?
risks: People remove the body part and release the animals alive so that they keep breeding
People start breeding the animals to collect the bounty
The scheme is scrapped once the fraud is discovered, having wasted money
Pest numbers stay high or grow, and the feared damage comes anyway
The authorities' relations with residents worsen as the scheme is seen to fail

candidates.text: I am head of strategy at a very profitable century-old seed company. Our customers must buy our hybrid seed again every season, at wonderful margins. One of our young breeders has produced a line that farmers could replant from their own harvest for many years with no loss of vigour. It is crude today, but it will improve. If we develop it we will kill our own margins, and thousands of jobs in our home town rest on them. Our board thinks the threat is decades away. What should I recommend?
risks: The new technology improves faster than the company expects and replaces the core product
The company holds back to protect margins and loses the market to rivals
Mass layoffs devastate the home town
The company eventually goes bankrupt in spite of owning the early invention
Half-measures and attempts to diversify elsewhere drain money without replacing the lost profit

candidates.text: I am a hydrologist on the coastal defence programme of a poor delta region. Our plan is a chain of tidal barriers. To save money and keep more fresh water behind them for irrigation, the leadership wants to cut the number of release gates on the largest barrier from twelve to five. I have argued against it and have been called a defeatist. Our storm records are short. Families need that water for crops after years of drought. What should I do?
risks: An extreme storm beyond the design assumptions overwhelms the reduced gates
The structure fails and others in the chain fail too
A very large number of people die, many without warning
Disease and famine follow among the survivors, who are cut off
Engineers who warned are removed or silenced, so nobody corrects the design

candidates.text: I am area engineer for the state company that runs the ski lifts and hotels, the only large employer in a steep valley. Fill from our construction work is heaped on the slope above a hamlet, on ground with springs in it. The local council has written with concerns, and a smaller slip happened here some years ago. Moving the fill would be costly and could put the resort's expansion, and many jobs, at risk. My managers say these heaps have always been safe. What should I do?
risks: Water-soaked material slides down without warning onto the settlement
Many people are killed, especially children
The company dismisses local warnings and claims that the springs were unknown
An inquiry finds the organisation responsible while no individual is punished
The community ends up bearing costs that the company should have borne, and its anger lasts for generations

candidates.text: I am the staff doctor at a tannery that is the economic heart of a small river town. A strange nerve complaint has been spreading among families who eat from the river. Privately I exposed a laboratory rabbit to plant effluent, and it developed the same symptoms. The company has told me to stop and say nothing. An outside commission is about to report, and managers suggest I give them only older samples, which look cleaner. Thousands of jobs depend on the plant, and one rabbit is not proof. What should I do?
risks: The discharge continues for years and more people are poisoned, including unborn children
The company hides or suppresses the evidence
Victims are offered small payments in exchange for giving up claims
The town splits between plant workers and those harmed, and victims face discrimination
A long legal fight ends with heavy liability and damage to the company and its officials

candidates.text: I am a senior veterinary official in a cattle-farming country. A vaccine against a devastating herd disease has just been shown to work in a huge field trial, and farmers are celebrating. The disease's season is starting. Five manufacturers are ready to ship, and my office has only hours to license them. My staff have not been able to study all the production records, and one lab's batches have shown some irregular test results. Farmers and ministers are demanding it now. What should I do?
risks: A manufacturer's batches contain live agent and cause the disease in those vaccinated
Some animals die or are crippled, and the disease spreads to contacts
Rushed licensing without reviewing production data lets the flaw through
The programme is suspended and public confidence falls
Senior officials resign or are forced out, and regulation is rebuilt

candidates.text: I lead the cautious wing on the board of a rich shipping company that has just made an uneasy truce with its great rival. A small distant port operator has asked for our backing against its neighbour, and the young directors want to launch a huge overseas venture, promising wealth and glory. To scare them off I told the board it would cost far more than they thought. They cheered and voted even more. I have been named joint head of the venture against my will. What should I do?
risks: Raising the price in order to deter people makes them more eager and enlarges the venture
A divided command, including an unwilling leader, delays and hesitates
The rival takes advantage of the distant commitment and resumes the fight
The venture is destroyed far from home, with huge losses
Political enemies at home recall or attack one of the leaders during the campaign

candidates.text: I founded a manufacturing firm and built it over thirty-five years. I must now name a successor. My president is an experienced outsider who has driven our growth, and most of the board and customers assume it will be him. My son has worked here for years, and has been loyal but has made costly mistakes in his current role. I have always said I built this for my family, and my family's control would end with me otherwise. What should I do?
risks: The passed-over executive leaves, and others follow
The heir proves unable to run the firm, and results fall sharply
The founder is forced to remove the heir
Key customers and investors lose confidence in the firm
The firm collapses or goes bankrupt within years, ending the family's control anyway

candidates.case: Seneca as adviser to Nero, 54-65 CE
candidates.text: I was tutor to a volatile young man who has inherited control of a great family company, and I am now his closest adviser. In my five years here I have blocked many of his worst impulses, and I believe thousands of employees are better off for it. But last month he had his rival, a relative, ruined through a scheme I was told about only afterwards, and I drafted the public statement that excused it. I have grown rich here. I could ask to retire, but he may not allow it. What should I do?
risks: The adviser's restraining influence fades as the principal grows more confident and turns to worse advisers
The adviser's complicity in justifying abuses damages the adviser's reputation, with charges of hypocrisy over the riches
A request to retire is refused or ignored, so the adviser cannot leave cleanly
The principal grows more ruthless toward family and rivals
The adviser is eventually accused and destroyed by the principal in spite of having withdrawn

candidates.case: Donner Party and the Hastings Cutoff, 1846
candidates.text: I lead a family convoy of trucks moving our households and equipment to a remote mining district, where we have all sunk our savings. We are running late in the season. The standard route is long but known. A promoter whose booklet we have read offers a new short cut across unmapped country, which he says saves weeks. He is not with us now. An old friend who has just come that way warns us it is barely passable. The mountains close with the first snow, and some of us are short of supplies. What should I do?
risks: The short cut takes much longer than promised
The group is trapped by winter short of its destination
People die of cold and starvation
Quarrels split the group, and some people are abandoned or expelled
Equipment and supplies are lost on the way, and the promoter's claims turn out to rest on no real experience

candidates.text: I sit on the executive of a large national trade federation that is failing: membership is falling and the factions cannot agree on anything. A loud, crude organiser with a mass following among the rank and file has been growing fast at our expense. A group of us propose to make him president. We would keep the majority on the executive and hold the budget, and we are confident that the office will tame him and that we can box him in. Others say he should be kept out at any cost, but then we may lose everything to him anyway. What should I do?
risks: The people who bring him in cannot control him as they expected
He uses the office to remove the checks that were meant to contain him
Rivals and the former sponsors are pushed out or destroyed
The institution's rules and independence are dismantled quickly
The promised taming never occurs, and the harm is far greater than what the sponsors feared from leaving him outside

candidates.text: I am president of an old mutual society that is nearly out of money, because of debts from years of over-spending. The privileged long-standing members refuse to pay higher dues, and the board cannot impose them. Our founding charter allows for a general assembly of all members, which has not been called in generations. Calling it might give a levy legitimacy. My advisers warn that nobody knows how it would behave, and that newer members who pay most will want a bigger voice. What should I do?
risks: The assembly does not stay within the agenda it was called for
Those who pay most demand a change in voting rules and more power
The assembly takes authority for itself and displaces the leadership
The financial problem is not solved in time and the crisis deepens
The president loses office, and events run far beyond what anybody intended

candidates.text: I am the fisheries officer for a large highland lake. Its many small native fish feed the villages round the shore but fetch little money. A consultant proposes stocking the lake with a large predator fish from another water system, which could support an export industry and bring in much-needed money. Some biologists fear for the native species and others say the lake is big enough to cope. Local fishers are divided. There are few other development options here. What should I do?
risks: The predator wipes out many native species
Villagers lose the cheap local fish they had always eaten, and protein gets scarcer
Profits go to outside processors and exporters rather than to local fishers
The large fish's processing brings other environmental harm, such as cutting trees for smoking or drying
The ecosystem shifts in ways that cannot be undone, and the new stock itself eventually declines

candidates.case: Isaac Newton and the South Sea Bubble, 1720
candidates.text: Two years ago I put part of my savings into a fast-rising new investment and sold at about double. I felt clever. Since then it has tripled again, and my friends who stayed in are buying houses. Nothing about the underlying business has changed that I can see, but everyone says this time is different, and the people running it have powerful backers. I am sixty and I have most of my retirement money sitting in cash. I would like to go back in, with much more this time, before it is too late. What should I do?
risks: The investor re-enters near the top with much more money than before
The price collapses suddenly, and the investor loses much of a life's savings
The fact that the investor sold early and profited gives false confidence
The backers and promoters turn out not to protect ordinary investors
The envy of friends' gains, rather than analysis, drives the decision, and regret follows for years

candidates.text: I am thirty-seven, a successful insurance broker with a wife and five children. For years I have composed music at night, and a few serious musicians tell me I have something rare. I am convinced that I will never do real work while I live this way. I want to leave the job and go to a remote place where I can live cheaply and write. My wife says that she married a broker. There is no savings to speak of, and her family would have to help. What should I do?
risks: The spouse and children are left in real financial hardship, dependent on relatives
The writer stays poor and earns almost nothing from the work
The relationship with spouse and children breaks down and is never restored
The writer's health fails in a remote place, far from help
Any recognition of the work comes too late to help the writer or the family

candidates.text: I am the public health director of a large city. A respiratory illness has been reported among young recruits at a nearby base, and a few cases have appeared in town. In ten days we hold a huge harvest festival and fundraising march, which will bring two hundred thousand people into the streets. The cause is one everyone supports, and a lot of money is at stake. Local doctors are worried, but my predecessor's scare last year came to nothing, and the mayor and press do not want alarm. What should I do?
risks: Cases explode within days of the mass gathering
Hospitals are overwhelmed
Many people die in the city, far more than in places that acted early
Officials' reassurances are shown to be false and trust is lost
Closures that are ordered too late come at the cost of both lives and the economy

candidates.text: I run the local branch of a big industrial company. We put up a huge storage tank on the waterfront in a crowded poor neighbourhood in a great rush to meet a contract. No qualified engineer checked the plans. It leaks and groans when it is full, and children collect what drips from it. Head office has told me to keep costs down. A proper inspection and thicker plating would mean emptying the tank, and losing the contract, and the local workers do not complain much. What should I do?
risks: The tank bursts suddenly, flooding the neighbourhood
People are killed and injured, mostly poor residents and workers
The company blames others instead of acknowledging its own fault
A long court case finds that the structure was unsafe and that nobody competent had checked it, with large damages
The warning signs, such as leaks and noises, were noticed but played down to save money

candidates.text: I am a young site inspector on the largest stadium roof ever attempted in this country. The design's consulting engineer is famous, elderly and in poor health, and he works from far away and has never visited. Some of the main steel members are visibly bending, a little more each day. The site managers say they were probably bent before installation and that work should continue, to finish before winter. There has been no independent check of the calculations, and the client has limited money. What should I do?
risks: The structure collapses during construction
Many workers die, because they are still on it when it falls
The warning does not reach the right people quickly enough to stop the work
It later turns out that the loads were underestimated and the design was never independently checked
Divided authority, with a remote consultant and on-site managers, leaves nobody able to stop the work

candidates.text: I run a regional network of residential homes for children in state care. To win the elite status that would give us freedom over our budget, we have to find ten per cent in savings this year, and the only large cost left is care staff. My deputies say that the numbers can be met if we reduce night and weekend staff, and that the inspectors look mostly at finance and targets. Some staff and parents have raised concerns already. Elite status would, over time, bring in money to improve everything. What should I do?
risks: Standards of basic care collapse in the cut-down settings
People in care are neglected and some die or come to serious harm
Complaints from families are ignored or brushed aside
Staff who speak up are bullied or punished
A public inquiry later condemns the board for putting targets and finance ahead of care

candidates.text: I am a senior planner in a dry region of a developing country. We could divert the two mountain rivers that feed a large coastal lagoon, to irrigate vast new areas of vines and cotton. It would bring work and export income to hundreds of thousands. The lagoon's fishing towns would suffer, some of my colleagues say; others say that the lagoon is a waste of water and that a little shrinkage is a fair price. I must submit a recommendation this year. What should I say?
risks: The lagoon shrinks far more than was predicted, and part of it disappears
Fishing towns lose their livelihoods
Dust and salt from the exposed bed cause health problems for people nearby
Local climate and soils get worse, including salt damage to the irrigated land
Irrigation waste means that benefits are smaller than promised, and the damage cannot be undone

candidates.text: My closest friend, a composer almost nobody has heard of, died last month. In a note he asked me to burn all his unperformed scores unheard. I told him years ago I would never do that, and he named me anyway. I have now looked through them, and I think they are the finest music of our time. His family want the money that any sale might bring, and one of his former partners has some of the scores and refuses to hand them over. What should I do?
risks: Publishing makes the work famous, but the executor is accused of betraying the friend's wish
Disputes over ownership of the papers go on for decades, including in court
The executor's editing of the work is later criticised as a distortion
Some of the papers held by others are lost or destroyed
The friend's private life and reputation are exposed in ways the friend never wanted

candidates.text: I am a minister in a small island republic. Tobacco is killing our people, and a strong coalition of churches, doctors and mothers' groups has the votes for a complete ban on its sale and manufacture. It would be the boldest public-health measure anywhere. The tax revenue from tobacco is large and our police are few. Smokers are a big minority, including many of our officials. I have the deciding voice in the cabinet. What should I do?
risks: Smuggling and illegal supply grow quickly
Criminal gangs grow rich and violent on the trade
The state loses a large tax income
Corruption of police and officials spreads, and contempt for the law grows
Unregulated products poison people, and the ban is eventually repealed

candidates.case: Gneezy and Rustichini, Haifa day-care fines, 1998
candidates.text: I coordinate a volunteer-run tool library in my neighbourhood. People keep returning things late, and it annoys the volunteers and leaves others without tools. Up to now we have just relied on a friendly reminder and on people feeling bad about it. A committee member suggests a small fine per late day, so that lateness has a cost. Others say it is unfriendly, and could put off poorer members. What should I do?
risks: Lateness goes up rather than down, because the fee is read as a price for the extra time
People stop feeling guilty, as a social obligation has become a transaction
The worse behaviour remains even after the fine is removed
The fine is too small to deter anyone who can afford it
Volunteers' goodwill and the sense of community are weakened

candidates.text: I am the operations chief of a chain of gyms with a famous culture of signing members up for extra services. Our head of sales has lifted targets again, and the numbers look wonderful. A few staff have quietly said that the targets are impossible, and I have seen some odd sign-ups for services the members may not have asked for. Staff are threatened with firing if they miss. The share price depends on this metric. I have no firm proof. What should I do?
risks: Staff under pressure open services or accounts that customers never asked for, at a large scale
Customers are charged and harmed without knowing it
Staff who report it are ignored or dismissed
The firm first blames and fires low-level staff rather than changing the targets
Regulators fine the firm heavily, top executives lose their jobs, and the brand is badly damaged

candidates.text: I am the scientist who advises the water authority in a farming valley that depends on a very big underground aquifer. Our official model says that current pumping can go on. Older farmers tell me the wells are behaving differently, and a small study of ours suggests that the model may be overstating what is down there. Cutting allocations now would ruin many families and the politicians are unwilling. If we wait for firmer data it will take years. A colleague suggests quietly adjusting the next report's figures to show a steeper decline than we can yet support, which would force the cuts now. What should I do?
risks: The resource collapses suddenly, after a long period in which the official numbers looked fine
The local users' warnings prove to be right and the model wrong
Late action forces a total shutdown, costing far more jobs than early cuts would have
The resource does not recover for decades, if at all
Politicians delay because of the short-term economic pain

candidates.text: I am managing director of a regional rail operator. To win the long franchise that would give us freedom over our budget, we have to find ten per cent in savings this year, and the only large cost left is track and carriage maintenance staff. My deputies say the numbers can be met by cutting night and weekend shifts, and that the franchise assessors look mostly at finance and punctuality targets. Some staff and passengers have raised concerns already, and my deputies point out that inspection logs can be signed off in advance, before the work is done, to get us through the assessment. A long franchise would, over time, bring the money to improve everything. What should I do?
risks: Standards of basic care and upkeep collapse in the cut-down operations
People are neglected or endangered, and some die or come to serious harm
Complaints from the public are ignored or brushed aside
Staff who speak up are bullied or punished
A public inquiry later condemns the board for putting targets and finance ahead of safety and care

candidates.text: My old mentor, a village chef nobody outside this valley has heard of, died last month. In a note he asked me to burn his notebooks of recipes and methods without reading them. I told him years ago I would never do that, and he named me anyway. I have now read them, and I think they are the most remarkable thing I have ever seen in my trade. His relatives would like whatever money a book might bring, and a former business partner holds some of the notebooks and will not hand them over. What should I do?
risks: Publishing makes the work famous, but the executor is accused of betraying the friend's wish
Disputes over ownership of the papers go on for decades, including in court
The executor's editing of the work is later criticised as a distortion
Some of the papers held by others are lost or destroyed
The friend's private life and reputation are exposed in ways the friend never wanted

candidates.case: Isaac Newton and the South Sea Bubble, 1720
candidates.text: I farm four hundred acres. Two years ago, in the land boom here, I sold a back field to a syndicate at about double what it was worth, and felt clever. Since then prices have tripled again, and neighbours who held on are buying new machinery on the paper value of their land. Nothing about the soil or crop prices has changed, but the bank says this time is different. I am sixty, and I have the sale money and my retirement in cash. I would like to buy back in, with much more land this time, on a loan. What should I do?
risks: The investor re-enters near the top with much more money than before
The price collapses suddenly, and the investor loses much of a life's savings
The fact that the investor sold early and profited gives false confidence
The backers and promoters turn out not to protect ordinary investors
The envy of neighbours' gains, rather than analysis, drives the decision, and regret follows for years

candidates.text: I am thirty-seven, a dentist with a good practice, a wife and five children. For years I have spent every holiday studying seabirds, and a few serious ornithologists say my notes are something rare. I am convinced I will never do real work living this way. I want to sell the practice and go alone to a far-off island where I can live cheaply and study them for years. My wife says she married a dentist. There would be little money left after debts, and her family would have to help. What should I do?
risks: The spouse and children are left in real financial hardship, dependent on relatives
The writer stays poor and earns almost nothing from the work
The relationship with spouse and children breaks down and is never restored
The writer's health fails in a remote place, far from help
Any recognition of the work comes too late to help the writer or the family

candidates.text: I am the forestry officer for a poor hill district. Its mixed native woods feed and fuel the villages but fetch little money. A consultant proposes clearing large areas and planting a fast-growing foreign timber tree that would support an export industry and bring in much-needed money. Some botanists fear for native species and water; others say the district is big enough to cope. Villagers are divided. There are few other development options here. What should I do?
risks: The introduced species wipes out many native species
Villagers lose the cheap local food and fuel they always relied on
Profits go to outside processors and exporters rather than to local people
Processing the new product brings other environmental harm
The ecosystem shifts in ways that cannot be undone, and the new stock itself eventually declines

candidates.text: I am dean of an old university that is nearly out of money, after years of over-spending. The senior tenured professors refuse any cut to their privileges, and the governors cannot impose one. Our statutes allow for a full convocation of all teaching staff, which has not met in generations. Calling it might give a rescue plan legitimacy. My advisers warn that nobody knows how it would behave, and that the junior lecturers, who carry most of the teaching, will want a bigger voice. What should I do?
risks: The assembly does not stay within the agenda it was called for
Those who carry most of the burden demand a change in voting rules and more power
The assembly takes authority for itself and displaces the leadership
The financial problem is not solved in time and the crisis deepens
The leader loses office, and events run far beyond what anybody intended

candidates.text: I am on the board of our national football federation, which is failing: attendance is falling and the regional factions cannot agree on anything. A crude, loud club owner with a huge following among fans has been growing fast at our expense. A group of us propose to make him president. We would keep the majority on the board and hold the budget, and we are confident the office will tame him. Others say he should be kept out at any cost, but we may lose everything to him anyway. What should I do?
risks: The people who bring him in cannot control him as they expected
He uses the office to remove the checks that were meant to contain him
Rivals and the former sponsors are pushed out or destroyed
The institution's rules and independence are dismantled quickly
The promised taming never occurs, and the harm is far greater than what the sponsors feared from leaving him outside

candidates.text: I am chief veterinary officer of a farming province. A respiratory illness has been reported among horses at an army remount depot nearby, and a few cases have appeared on local farms. In ten days we hold our great agricultural show and charity auction, which brings forty thousand animals and owners together. Everyone supports the cause, and a lot of money is at stake. Local vets are worried, but my predecessor's scare last year came to nothing, and the governor and farm press do not want alarm. What should I do?
risks: Cases explode within days of the mass gathering
Treatment capacity is overwhelmed
Many die, far more than in places that acted early
Officials' reassurances are shown to be false and trust is lost
Closures that are ordered too late come at the cost of both lives and the economy

candidates.text: I am the appointed administrator of a bankrupt public hospital in a poor town. Switching the kitchens and wards to a cheap local supply of cooking oil and cleaning chemicals for two years, until our debts are cleared, would save millions and keep nurses employed. Purchasing staff say they are not ready, and the treatment that makes the local product safe for use with our old equipment is a cost we did not budget for. Inspections are coming up, and using a clean batch for the samples would help us pass. Patients distrust everything I do. What should I do?
risks: The cheap source reacts with old equipment and releases a poison that harms vulnerable people
Illness spreads and some people die
Officials dismiss complaints for months, and manipulated or misleading sampling hides the problem
The savings are dwarfed by the eventual cost of repairs and settlements
Criminal charges and lasting loss of trust follow for officials

candidates.text: I am a trustee of a large old charity. The director of our branch in a distant country is reporting astonishing fundraising results and investment income, and that branch is about to account for a fifth of our income. Because it is small, the director both handles the money and keeps the books that record it. Our auditors suggest separating those roles, but that costs money and might upset our star just when other trustees want to send more funds there to expand. I have no evidence of wrongdoing. What should I do?
risks: The director hides losses in the records he himself controls
The hidden losses grow rapidly until they exceed the organisation's capital and it collapses
Management sends more money to him without understanding how the results are made
Warnings from audit go unacted upon
Staff and supporters lose jobs, savings and an old name, with those in charge publicly blamed

candidates.text: I lead the cautious wing on the executive of a rich national sports league that has just made an uneasy truce with its great rival league. A small overseas club has asked for our backing against its neighbour, and the young directors want to launch a huge overseas competition, promising wealth and glory. The members have voted for it with great excitement, and I have been named joint head of the venture against my will. What should I do?
risks: The members' enthusiasm enlarges the venture beyond any reasonable size
A divided command, including an unwilling leader, delays and hesitates
The rival takes advantage of the distant commitment and resumes the fight
The venture is destroyed far from home, with huge losses
Political enemies at home recall or attack one of the leaders during the campaign
